patch.value:
## What is recorded, and where it can be read

`claim` and `release` are first-class recorded operations: 2,745 claim entries and 2,281 release entries across 2,258 history streams on this tracker today. The derived view of them is `claim_state`, and it is produced by `resolveClaimStateContext` (`src/sdk/query/get.ts:159`), which calls `readHistoryEntries` on one item's stream and folds the last claim and the last release out of it. That function is reachable from exactly one place: `pm get <id>`.

The consequence is a complexity claim, not a preference. Answering "which items does the fleet hold right now, and who holds each" requires one full history-stream read per item. On this corpus that is 2,258 stream reads over 42,771 entries for a single fleet-wide occupancy query. At the stated target of a million items with thousands of concurrent agents, this is the one question a fleet must answer continuously, and it is the only per-item read whose cost is O(stream length) rather than O(1).

## The collection surfaces cannot express it

`pm list` publishes 69 flags. None of them filters on claim state. The filter vocabulary it does publish for ownership is `--assignee` and `--assignee-filter`, which read the mutable `assignee` metadata field that `claim` happens to write — 288 items carry an assignee value, and none of those values distinguishes a live claim from an assignment recorded and long since released.

Projection is the same story from the other side. `pm list --full --json` returns 25 field keys; `claim_state` is not among them, and there is no `--fields claim_state` escape because `claim_state` is not a list projection group at all. `pm get` declares `claim_state`, `claim_state.claimed`, `claim_state.assignee` and `claim_state.last_claim` as selectable fields (`src/sdk/query/get.ts:258-270`). The single-item surface models occupancy precisely; every collection surface is blind to it.

## The status vocabulary that is queryable carries none of the signal

Measured across all 2,245 items: `draft` 0, `in_progress` 0, `blocked` 0, `open` 319, `closed` 1,913, `canceled` 13. Three of the six lifecycle statuses have never been used, and they are exactly the three that describe work in flight.

That is not an oversight in the corpus, it is a consequence of the design. The project models occupancy with claim/release and blocking with `blocked_by` edges, so `in_progress` and `blocked` never get written, even though `AGENTS.md`'s own quickstart instructs `pm update <id> --status in_progress --message "Start implementation"` at claim time. Two top-level commands, `pm list-in-progress` and `pm list-blocked`, are therefore provably empty on this workspace and on any workspace that follows the same guidance — a read surface whose answer is structurally always the empty set.

So both representations of "someone is working on this" are unusable at fleet scale, in opposite ways. The status field is filterable and empty. The claim fold is populated and unfilterable.

## Why this blocks work already planned

The fleet algorithms are written against an assumption that this defect falsifies. Catalog entry (24) on pm-4k6b, fleet-joint context diversification, states that the peer set "is approximated from state the workspace already records: the claim ledger says who holds what ... readable without new distributed machinery." The claim ledger does say who holds what. It is not readable without new machinery — reading it for N peers costs N stream folds. pm-3oqjnc must know current occupancy to allocate without collisions, and pm-tch9cs must know it to amortize assemblies across holders of related work. Each would independently rediscover the same missing primitive.

## Occupancy is interval-valued, and only the stream knows it

The fold keeps the last claim and the last release. The stream holds every claim and every release with timestamps and author identity, so occupancy is reconstructable as intervals over the whole history rather than as a boolean at now. Reconstructed on this corpus: 2,109 claim intervals during which the holder mutated the item, 25 intervals with no content mutation between claim and release, and 295 claims superseded by a later claim with no release between them. That distribution is a usable signal about contention and abandoned attempts, and today nothing can read it, for the same reason nothing can read current occupancy — there is no surface between "one item's fold" and "the raw stream".

This is the same class of loss that pm-4k6b's `state-erased-signal-recovery` entry describes for ordering edges: the fold is not information-preserving and the signal survives only in the append-only record. The remedy here is narrower, because nothing is deleted — the fold is simply not offered over collections.

## What this item owns

A collection-level occupancy surface: filterable (`--claimed`, `--held-by`, and their negations), projectable as a declared field group on the collection reads, and computed without one stream fold per item — which means occupancy must be maintained as derived index state alongside the other derived read state, not recomputed from history on every query. The interval reconstruction is the second half: an occupancy history read that returns claim intervals with holder identity and mutation-during-hold, so contention and abandonment become queryable rather than latent.

## Boundaries

Not the lifecycle-status question. Whether `in_progress` should be written at claim time is a product decision about the status vocabulary and belongs with the lifecycle-role work; this item is about making the signal that *is* recorded readable in bulk, whichever field ends up carrying it.

Not the allocation algorithm (pm-3oqjnc) and not the diversification algorithm (pm-4k6b entry 24). Both consume this; neither can supply it.

Not lock contention or claim throughput (pm-lvyd), which is about whether claiming works under load rather than about whether the resulting occupancy can be read.

Not `pm get`'s own corpus scan (pm-ydshl9). That is the cost of locating one item; this is the cost of folding one item's history once located, multiplied by the corpus.

Occupancy is a per-item history fold with no collection surface: reading which items a fleet holds costs one full history-stream read per item, while the three lifecycle statuses that are filterable are empty across all 2,245 items

claim_state is derived by resolveClaimStateContext (src/sdk/query/get.ts:159) folding readHistoryEntries over one item's stream, and it is reachable only from pm get. No collection surface filters or projects it: pm list publishes 69 flags and none is claim-aware, and --full returns 25 field keys without claim_state. The queryable ownership vocabulary is --assignee over a mutable metadata field that 288 items carry and that cannot distinguish a live claim from a released one. Meanwhile draft, in_progress and blocked are 0 across all 2,245 items, so pm list-in-progress and pm list-blocked are structurally empty. Answering 'what does the fleet hold right now' therefore costs 2,258 stream folds over 42,771 entries on this corpus, and O(corpus) stream reads at the million-item target. Duplicate check: searched claim/owner/fleet/who-is-working lineages and read pm-ugld, pm-lvyd, pm-0mhspz, pm-3oqjnc, pm-tch9cs, pm-ydshl9, pm-801d; none owns bulk occupancy readability.

Collection reads filter and project occupancy without one history fold per item; occupancy is served from maintained derived state; an occupancy-interval read returns claim intervals with holder identity and mutation-during-hold; fleet-wide occupancy query cost is independent of history length; pm-4k6b entry (24) peer-conditioning and pm-3oqjnc allocation both consume the same surface
Make live and historical occupancy readable in bulk so fleet algorithms have the input they already assume
Thousands of concurrent agents can see the work-front without O(corpus x stream) reads; contention and abandonment become queryable signals
